lessons.title: States of Matter
lessons.content:
Matter is anything that has mass and takes up space. It exists in three primary states: solid, liquid, and gas. According to the kinetic theory, all matter is made up of tiny particles that are in constant motion. In a solid, particles are closely packed in a regular arrangement and vibrate about fixed positions. In a liquid, they are still close but can move past each other, while in a gas, they are far apart and move rapidly in all directions.

Changes of state occur when energy is added or removed. Melting occurs when a solid is heated and its particles gain enough kinetic energy to break free from their fixed positions. Evaporation and boiling turn liquids into gases, while condensation and freezing reverse these processes. Sublimation is the rare process where a solid turns directly into a gas, such as with 'dry ice' (solid CO₂) or iodine.

On the CSEC Chemistry exam, you must be able to describe these states in terms of particle arrangement, movement, and energy. You may also be asked to interpret heating and cooling curves, identifying the melting and boiling points where the temperature remains constant as the state changes.

lessons.title: Atomic Structure
lessons.content:
The atom is the smallest unit of an element that retains its chemical properties. It consists of three main subatomic particles: protons, neutrons, and electrons. Protons (positively charged) and neutrons (neutral) are found in the dense centre called the nucleus. Electrons (negatively charged) orbit the nucleus in specific energy levels or shells.

An element is defined by its Atomic Number (Z), which is the number of protons in its nucleus. In a neutral atom, the number of electrons equals the number of protons. The Mass Number (A) is the total number of protons and neutrons. Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same atomic number but different mass numbers due to a different number of neutrons.

When writing the electronic configuration, electrons fill the shells starting from the one closest to the nucleus. For the first 20 elements, the shells can hold a maximum of 2, 8, 8, and 2 electrons respectively. Understanding atomic structure is vital for predicting how elements will react and bond with others.

Because isotopes of an element have the same number of electrons, they have identical chemical properties, but their different numbers of neutrons give them different masses, which is what makes them useful. Radioactive isotopes, called radioisotopes, are used as tracers: a small amount of a radioisotope is introduced into a system and its radiation is followed to track where the substance goes, for example through a plant or through a person's body.

Radioisotopes have further uses. Carbon-14 is used to date ancient remains, because it decays at a known rate after a living thing dies, and iodine-131 and cobalt-60 are used in medicine to treat disease and sterilise equipment. The same isotope that is useful can also be dangerous, because its radiation must be handled with shielding and kept away from living tissue.

lessons.title: Pure Substances and Mixtures
lessons.content:
Matter is either a pure substance or a mixture. A pure substance is made of only one kind of particle and has a fixed composition and a sharp melting and boiling point. An element is a pure substance that cannot be broken down into anything simpler by chemical means, and a compound is a pure substance made of two or more elements chemically joined in fixed proportions, such as water, H₂O.

A mixture contains two or more substances that are not chemically joined, so they keep their own properties and can be present in any proportion. The parts of a mixture can be separated by physical means such as filtration, evaporation or distillation, because no chemical reaction is needed. Air, sea water and crude oil are all mixtures.

To tell a pure substance from a mixture, test a sample's behaviour as it changes state. A pure substance melts and boils at one fixed temperature, while a mixture melts over a range of temperatures and often boils over a range too. Paper chromatography can also show that a single 'pure' spot separates into more than one coloured substance, proving it was a mixture.

lessons.title: Solutions, Suspensions, and Colloids
lessons.content:
A mixture of substances can take three common forms: a solution, a suspension or a colloid. They are told apart by the size of the particles mixed into the liquid and by what the mixture looks like. A solution is a homogeneous mixture in which the dissolved particles are single ions or molecules, far too small to see or to be trapped by filter paper, so the mixture is clear and does not settle on standing.

A suspension is a heterogeneous mixture in which the solid particles are large enough to be seen and to settle out when the mixture is left to stand, such as muddy water or chalk powder shaken in water. The particles are also large enough to be trapped by filter paper, so a suspension can be separated by filtration. A colloid sits between the two: its particles are larger than those of a solution but too small to settle, so the mixture looks cloudy but stable, as in milk or fog.

These differences come from particle size. A solution has the smallest particles and stays clear, a suspension has the largest particles and separates on standing, and a colloid has particles in between that scatter a beam of light, which is why a colloid can look cloudy while a true solution lets light pass straight through.

lessons.title: Solubility and Separation Techniques
lessons.content:
Solubility is the maximum mass of a solute that dissolves in a given mass of solvent at a given temperature, and it usually rises as the temperature rises. A saturated solution holds the maximum amount of solute at that temperature, so any extra solute will not dissolve, and a solubility curve is a graph of solubility against temperature used to predict how much will dissolve.

Different separation techniques suit different mixtures. Filtration separates an insoluble solid from a liquid, using filter paper that holds back the solid. Evaporation and crystallisation recover a dissolved solid by removing the solvent, while simple distillation separates a solvent from a solution by boiling and condensing the vapour, and fractional distillation separates two miscible liquids with different boiling points. Paper chromatography separates the different coloured solutes in a mixture because each solute travels up the paper at its own rate.

The right method depends on what is being separated. Filtration and evaporation work for a salt mixed with an insoluble solid or dissolved in water, crystallisation gives pure crystals from a saturated solution, distillation recovers the liquid, and chromatography separates and identifies the colours in a mixture such as an ink or a food dye.

lessons.title: Sucrose Extraction
lessons.content:
Sucrose is the sugar extracted from sugar cane, and its production is the Caribbean's most familiar industrial chemical process. The first step is to crush the harvested cane between rollers and press out the juice, leaving a fibrous residue called bagasse. The juice is then clarified by adding lime, which neutralises its acidity and causes impurities to settle out.

The clarified juice is heated to evaporate much of the water, concentrating it into a thick syrup, and this syrup is boiled until crystals of raw sugar form. The mixture of crystals and syrup is spun in a centrifuge to separate the brown crystals from the syrup, which is drained off as molasses. The raw sugar crystals are then refined by re-dissolving them, filtering, and re-crystallising to give white sugar.

CSEC uses sucrose extraction as the example of a large-scale separation process, because it joins several techniques together in order: crushing, clarification, evaporation, crystallisation and separation. At each stage a physical separation removes one part of the mixture, so no chemical reaction is needed to obtain the sugar from the cane.

Identify the separation technique used at each stage
Explain why sucrose extraction is a physical rather than a chemical process

lessons.title: Periodic Table Trends
lessons.content:
The Periodic Table is an organised arrangement of all known chemical elements, ordered by increasing atomic number. Elements are arranged in vertical columns called 'Groups' and horizontal rows called 'Periods.' Elements in the same group have the same number of valence (outer shell) electrons, which gives them similar chemical properties.

Several important trends appear across the table. Atomic radius generally decreases from left to right across a period because the increasing nuclear charge pulls the electrons closer. Conversely, it increases down a group as more energy levels are added. Electronegativity (the ability to attract electrons) and ionisation energy (the energy needed to remove an electron) both tend to increase across a period and decrease down a group.

CSEC Chemistry often focuses on Group 1 (Alkali Metals), Group 7 (Halogens), and Group 0 (Noble Gases). Group 1 metals become more reactive as you go down the group because the outer electron is further from the nucleus and easier to lose. Group 7 non-metals become less reactive down the group as it becomes harder to attract an electron.

The position of an element in the table lets you predict its properties before you ever see it. An element in the same group as a known element has the same number of valence electrons and so behaves in a similar way, and an element in the same period has its outer electrons in the same shell, so its properties change in a regular way across the period.

To predict a property, find the element's group and period and apply the trend. From its group you can predict how many electrons it will gain, lose or share and its likely formula, and from its position you can predict whether it is a metal or a non-metal and how reactive it is likely to be. This is why the table is used to work out the properties of an element such as an alkali metal or a halogen, even one the student has never handled.

lessons.title: Ionic and Covalent Bonding
lessons.content:
Chemical bonding is the process by which atoms combine to achieve a stable electron configuration, usually a full outer shell. Ionic bonding occurs between metals and non-metals through the transfer of electrons. The metal atom loses electrons to become a positive ion (cation), while the non-metal gains them to become a negative ion (anion). The resulting electrostatic attraction between these oppositely charged ions forms an ionic lattice.

Covalent bonding occurs between non-metal atoms through the sharing of pairs of electrons. A single covalent bond consists of one shared pair. Simple covalent molecules, like water (H₂O) or methane (CH₄), have strong internal bonds but weak intermolecular forces, leading to low melting points. Giant covalent structures, like diamond or graphite, have extensive networks of strong bonds, making them very hard or high-melting.

You will be expected to draw 'dot-and-cross' diagrams to illustrate both types of bonding. Remember that for ionic bonds, you show the ions in brackets with their charges, while for covalent bonds, you show the overlap of the outer shells where the electrons are shared.

The properties of a substance follow from the structure of its crystals. An ionic lattice is a regular repeating arrangement of oppositely charged ions held by strong electrostatic forces, so ionic compounds are hard and have high melting and boiling points, and they conduct electricity only when molten or dissolved, because only then are the ions free to move.

Giant covalent structures have their atoms joined by covalent bonds throughout, which gives them high melting points, while simple covalent molecules have strong bonds inside each molecule but only weak forces between molecules, which is why they have low melting points. Comparing structure to property in this way lets you explain why one substance is hard, another conducts, and a third is a gas at room temperature.

Allotropy is the existence of the same element in more than one form in the same physical state, and carbon is the classic example. Diamond and graphite are both pure carbon, yet diamond is hard, transparent and an electrical insulator, while graphite is soft, grey and a conductor of electricity, because their carbon atoms are arranged differently.

In diamond each carbon atom is bonded to four others in a rigid three-dimensional network, which makes diamond the hardest natural substance and gives it a very high melting point. In graphite each carbon atom is bonded to only three others in flat layers, and the fourth electron of each atom is delocalised, which lets graphite conduct electricity and lets the layers slide over one another, which is why graphite is used as a lubricant and in pencil lead.

lessons.title: Metallic Bonding
lessons.content:
Metallic bonding holds the atoms of a metal together. Each metal atom gives up its outer electrons, so the metal becomes a lattice of positive ions arranged in regular layers, surrounded by a 'sea' of delocalised electrons that are free to move throughout the structure. The metal is held together by the strong electrostatic attraction between these positive ions and the sea of delocalised electrons.

The sea of delocalised electrons explains the properties of metals. Metals conduct electricity because the electrons can move and carry charge through the metal, and they conduct heat for the same reason, since the moving electrons pass energy along. Metals are malleable and ductile because the layers of positive ions can slide over one another without the bonding breaking, so the metal can be hammered into shape or drawn into a wire.

The strength of metallic bonding grows with the number of delocalised electrons each atom contributes and with the charge on the ions, which is why metals differ in their melting points and hardness. An alloy, in which atoms of another element are mixed into the layers, is usually harder than the pure metal because the different-sized atoms stop the layers from sliding as easily.

lessons.title: Molar Mass and Calculations
lessons.content:
The mole is the standard unit in chemistry for measuring the amount of a substance. One mole contains exactly 6.022 × 10²³ particles (Avogadro's constant). The molar mass (M) of a substance is the mass of one mole of that substance, expressed in grams per mole (g/mol). It is numerically equal to the relative atomic mass or relative molecular mass of the substance.

The fundamental formula for mole calculations is: Number of moles (n) = Mass (m) / Molar Mass (M). For example, the molar mass of water (H₂O) is approximately 18 g/mol (1×2 for H + 16 for O). Therefore, 36 grams of water is exactly 2 moles.

In the CSEC exam, you will use moles to solve stoichiometry problems, such as determining the mass of product formed from a given mass of reactant. This requires a balanced chemical equation to find the molar ratio between substances. Practise these calculations until you can move confidently between mass, moles, and the number of particles.

Stoichiometry uses the balanced equation to work out the masses of substances that react together. The coefficients in the balanced equation give the molar ratio, so the ratio of the moles of the reactants and products is fixed, and from the moles of one substance the moles of every other substance can be found.

A reacting-mass calculation has three steps. First, convert the given mass to moles with n = m / M. Then use the molar ratio from the equation to find the moles of the substance asked for. Finally, convert those moles back to a mass with m = n x M. This sequence is used to predict the mass of product formed from a given mass of reactant and the mass of reactant needed to make a given mass of product.

lessons.title: Avogadro's Law
lessons.content:
Avogadro's law states that equal volumes of all gases, at the same temperature and pressure, contain the same number of molecules. It follows from the law that one mole of any gas occupies the same volume under the same conditions, and this volume is called the molar volume. At room temperature and pressure, the molar volume of a gas is about 24 cubic decimetres, written 24 dm³.

The molar volume links the volume of a gas to the amount in moles. The relationship is: amount in moles (n) equals volume divided by the molar volume, so 48 dm³ of any gas at room temperature and pressure contains 2 moles, and 24 dm³ contains 1 mole. This works for every gas because the distance between the molecules is so much larger than the molecules themselves that their own size makes no difference.

Avogadro's law is used in calculations with reacting gases. When a balanced equation shows the reacting volumes, the ratio of the volumes of the gases equals the ratio of the moles in the equation, so one volume of hydrogen reacts with half a volume of oxygen to form water vapour in a fixed whole-number ratio.

lessons.title: Chemical Equations and Conservation of Matter
lessons.content:
A chemical equation describes a reaction using formulae, with the reactants on the left and the products on the right of an arrow. The equation must be balanced so that the number of atoms of each element is the same on both sides, because in a chemical reaction atoms are neither created nor destroyed, only rearranged. This is the law of conservation of mass.

To balance an equation, place numbers, called coefficients, in front of the formulae, never change the formulae themselves. For example, hydrogen reacts with oxygen to form water, and the unbalanced equation H₂ + O₂ → H₂O becomes 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, so there are four hydrogen atoms and two oxygen atoms on each side.

The conservation of mass has a practical meaning: the total mass of the reactants equals the total mass of the products. In a reaction that seems to lose mass, such as one that gives off a gas, the missing mass has escaped into the air, and if the gas is collected the mass is found to be unchanged.

lessons.title: pH Scale and Indicators
lessons.content:
The pH scale is a logarithmic scale ranging from 0 to 14, used to measure the acidity or alkalinity of a solution. A pH of 7 is neutral (like pure water). Solutions with a pH less than 7 are acidic, while those with a pH greater than 7 are basic (alkaline). The further a value is from 7, the stronger the acid or base.

Indicators are substances that change colour depending on the pH of the solution they are in. Litmus paper is a simple indicator: it turns red in acids and blue in bases. Universal indicator is more precise, providing a full spectrum of colours (Red-Orange-Yellow-Green-Blue-Indigo-Violet) that correspond to specific pH values from 1 to 14.

Understanding pH is essential for many biological and industrial processes. In the laboratory, you might use a pH meter for high precision or various indicators like phenolphthalein or methyl orange during titrations. CSEC questions often ask you to identify the pH range of common household substances or predict colour changes in specific indicators.

An acid and a base are defined by the ions they form in water. An acid is a substance that produces hydrogen ions, H⁺, when dissolved in water, and a base is a substance that produces hydroxide ions, OH⁻, when dissolved in water. An alkali is a soluble base, so every alkali is a base but not every base is an alkali.

This definition ties directly to the pH scale. The more hydrogen ions a solution contains, the lower its pH and the stronger the acid, while a base lowers the concentration of hydrogen ions and raises the pH. Neutralisation is then the reaction in which hydrogen ions and hydroxide ions join to form water, which is why the pH of a solution moves towards 7 as an acid and a base neutralise each other.

lessons.title: Neutralisation and Salt Formation
lessons.content:
Neutralisation is a chemical reaction between an acid and a base (or alkali) to produce a salt and water. The general equation is: Acid + Base → Salt + Water. For example, Hydrochloric acid reacts with Sodium hydroxide to form Sodium chloride (table salt) and water: HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O.

The 'salt' produced depends on the specific acid and base used. Hydrochloric acid produces chlorides, sulphuric acid produces sulphates, and nitric acid produces nitrates. If the base is a carbonate, the reaction also produces carbon dioxide gas: Acid + Metal Carbonate → Salt + Water + Carbon Dioxide.

Titration is the common laboratory technique used to find the exact volume of acid needed to neutralise a set volume of base. A burette is used to add one reactant to the other until an indicator shows the reaction is complete. This topic is a favourite for CSEC practical and paper 2 questions, often requiring you to calculate concentrations from titration data.

Acids react with several classes of substance in addition to bases and carbonates. An acid reacts with a reactive metal to give a salt and hydrogen gas, for example hydrochloric acid with zinc to give zinc chloride and hydrogen, and the test for the hydrogen is a lighted splint that gives a squeaky pop.

An acid also reacts with a metal oxide or a metal hydroxide to give a salt and water only, for example sulphuric acid with copper(II) oxide to give copper(II) sulphate and water. Each reaction follows the same pattern of producing a salt, so the salt formed can be predicted by knowing which acid supplies its negative ion and which metal supplies its positive ion.

Volumetric analysis uses titration to find the concentration of an unknown solution. A known volume of one solution is measured into a flask, an indicator is added, and the other solution is run in from a burette until the indicator changes colour at the end point, when the two solutions have reacted exactly.

The titration calculation uses the volumes and one known concentration. From the concentration and volume of one solution its amount in moles is found with n = c x V, the mole ratio from the equation gives the moles of the other solution, and dividing by its volume gives its concentration. The titre is the volume read from the burette, and repeating the titration until concordant results agree makes the answer reliable.

lessons.title: Salt Preparation
lessons.content:
A salt is an ionic compound formed when the hydrogen of an acid is replaced by a metal or by an ammonium ion. The method used to prepare a salt depends on whether it is soluble in water and on the starting materials. A soluble salt of an unreactive metal is made by reacting an acid with a metal, a metal oxide, a metal hydroxide or a metal carbonate, then crystallising the salt from the resulting solution.

Several routes lead to a salt. An acid reacts with a metal to give a salt and hydrogen gas, with a metal oxide or hydroxide to give a salt and water, and with a carbonate to give a salt, water and carbon dioxide. A salt whose two reactants are both soluble, and where neither gives a sign that the reaction is complete, is made by titration, in which the two solutions are mixed until neutral.

An insoluble salt is prepared by precipitation, which mixes two soluble salt solutions so that the insoluble salt forms as a solid and is then collected by filtration and dried. The choice of route is decided by solubility: soluble salts use an acid reaction or titration, and insoluble salts use precipitation.

lessons.title: Uses and Dangers of Salts
lessons.content:
Salts are valuable in food, farming and industry. Common salt, sodium chloride, flavours and preserves food, and ammonium salts supply the nitrogen in fertilisers. Sodium hydrogencarbonate is a raising agent in baking, and calcium sulphate is used in plaster and plaster of Paris, while many other salts are used in industry to make products such as glass, soap and dyes.

Salts also carry dangers that must be managed. Some salts are toxic if swallowed, and heavy-metal salts such as those of lead and mercury are poisonous and must be kept out of food and water. Soluble fertiliser salts washed off farmland can build up in rivers and lakes, and excessive salt in the diet raises blood pressure, so salt is used in the smallest amount that does the job.

The same salt can be a benefit in one place and a hazard in another, so its use depends on the amount and the setting. Sodium chloride preserves food and de-ices roads yet corrodes metal and damages plants at high concentration, which is why safe handling and correct dosage matter as much as the salt's usefulness.

Describe the dangers posed by toxic and heavy-metal salts
Explain how one salt can be both useful and hazardous

lessons.title: Defining Redox
lessons.content:
Redox (reduction-oxidation) reactions involve the transfer of electrons between chemical species. Oxidation is defined as the loss of electrons, while reduction is the gain of electrons. A helpful mnemonic is OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain.

In any redox reaction, one substance is oxidised while another is reduced. The substance that accepts electrons and causes another to be oxidised is called the 'oxidising agent' (it gets reduced itself). The substance that don'tates electrons and causes another to be reduced is the 'reducing agent' (it gets oxidised itself). Oxidation numbers are often used to track these changes; an increase in oxidation number indicates oxidation, while a decrease indicates reduction.

Common redox examples include the rusting of iron, the combustion of fuels, and the reactions in batteries. You will be asked to identify which species are being oxidised or reduced in a given equation and to write half-equations to show the movement of electrons.

Common oxidising agents accept electrons and are themselves reduced, while common reducing agents donate electrons and are themselves oxidised. Familiar oxidising agents include oxygen, the halogens such as chlorine, and acidified potassium manganate(VII), which changes colour from purple to colourless as it is reduced.

Familiar reducing agents include hydrogen, carbon, carbon monoxide and reactive metals such as sodium. Hydrogen removes oxygen from metal oxides to give the metal, and carbon does the same in the extraction of metals, while a reactive metal gives up its electrons to a less reactive metal ion in a displacement reaction. Identifying the oxidising and reducing substances in a given reaction is a standard CSEC skill.
objectives: Define oxidation and reduction in terms of electron transfer
Identify oxidising and reducing agents
Name common oxidising agents and common reducing agents
Identify which substance is oxidised and which is reduced in a reaction
concepts: OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain (of electrons).
Oxidising agents accept electrons and are themselves reduced, such as oxygen, chlorine and acidified potassium manganate(VII).
Reducing agents donate electrons and are themselves oxidised, such as hydrogen, carbon, carbon monoxide and reactive metals.

lessons.title: Conduction and Electrolytes
lessons.content:
Substances conduct electricity in two different ways. Metals conduct by the movement of electrons, while ionic compounds conduct only when their ions are free to move, which happens when the compound is molten or dissolved in water. A compound that conducts electricity when molten or in aqueous solution, and is decomposed by it, is called an electrolyte, and the conduction is called electrolytic conduction.

An electrolyte is made of ions, and in the liquid state these ions are free to move towards the electrodes. Sodium chloride does not conduct when solid, because its ions are held in a fixed lattice and cannot move, but molten sodium chloride and sodium chloride solution both conduct. A covalent substance such as sugar dissolves without forming ions, so its solution does not conduct, and it is a non-electrolyte.

Electrolytic conduction is always accompanied by chemical change, because the current decomposes the electrolyte. This is the key difference from metallic conduction, in which the same electrons simply pass through the metal without changing it. Electrolytes include molten salts, salt solutions, acids and alkalis, while non-electrolytes include sugar solution, pure water and covalent liquids such as ethanol.
objectives: Describe how metals and electrolytes conduct electricity
Distinguish an electrolyte from a non-electrolyte
Explain why an ionic compound conducts only when molten or dissolved

Ionic compounds conduct only when their ions are free to move, which happens when molten or dissolved in water.
Non-electrolyte: a substance such as sugar that dissolves without forming ions, so its solution does not conduct.

lessons.title: Electrolysis Principles
lessons.content:
Electrolysis is the decomposition of a molten or dissolved ionic compound by passing an electric current through it. The current enters and leaves through two electrodes, which are usually made of graphite or platinum because these are inert, and the electrode joined to the negative terminal of the supply is the cathode while the one joined to the positive terminal is the anode.

During electrolysis the ions move towards the oppositely charged electrodes. Positive ions, called cations, move to the cathode and gain electrons there, which is reduction, while negative ions, called anions, move to the anode and lose electrons there, which is oxidation. An ion becomes a neutral atom or molecule when it is discharged at an electrode, and this discharge happens at the electrode with the opposite charge.

Electrolysis of a molten binary compound gives its two elements. Molten lead(II) bromide forms lead at the cathode and bromine at the anode, because the lead ions are reduced to lead metal and the bromide ions are oxidised to bromine. The process therefore drives a redox reaction using electrical energy.
objectives: Define electrolysis and identify the cathode and the anode
Describe the movement and discharge of cations and anions
Explain the products of the electrolysis of a molten binary compound
concepts: Electrolysis: the decomposition of a molten or dissolved ionic compound by passing an electric current through it.
Cathode: the electrode joined to the negative terminal, where cations are reduced; anode: the electrode joined to the positive terminal, where anions are oxidised.
Cations move to the cathode and gain electrons, anions move to the anode and lose electrons.

lessons.title: Factors Affecting Electrolysis
lessons.content:
When an electrolyte in solution contains more than one kind of positive or negative ion, the ion that is discharged at an electrode is decided by several factors. The position of the ion in the reactivity series matters most: the less reactive a metal, the more easily its ion is discharged at the cathode, so in an aqueous solution the hydrogen from water is discharged before a reactive metal such as sodium, while copper is discharged before hydrogen.

Concentration also matters, because a more concentrated ion is more likely to be discharged. In dilute sodium chloride solution, the hydroxide ions from water are oxidised at the anode to give oxygen, but in concentrated sodium chloride solution the chloride ions are discharged to give chlorine. The nature of the electrode can matter too, because some electrodes are inert while others take part in the reaction.

At the cathode in an aqueous solution, hydrogen is produced if the metal is above hydrogen in the reactivity series, and the metal is produced if it is below hydrogen. At the anode, oxygen is usually produced from dilute solutions unless the anion is a halide, in which case the halogen is produced instead. Position in the series, concentration and the electrode material together decide the products.
objectives: Explain how position in the reactivity series decides which ion is discharged
Describe the effect of concentration on the products of electrolysis
Predict the products at the cathode and the anode in an aqueous solution

A more concentrated ion is more likely to be discharged, so concentrated sodium chloride solution gives chlorine at the anode.

lessons.title: Faraday Constant and Calculations
lessons.content:
The amount of a substance produced at an electrode depends on the quantity of electricity that passes through the electrolyte. The quantity of electricity, or charge, is measured in coulombs and is the product of the current in amperes and the time in seconds, so charge Q equals current I times time t, written Q = I t.

The Faraday constant links charge to moles of electrons. One mole of electrons carries a charge of 96 500 coulombs, and this value is the Faraday constant, F. It follows that the number of moles of electrons transferred equals the charge divided by 96 500, and because one mole of silver ions needs one mole of electrons to form one mole of silver, a charge of 96 500 coulombs deposits exactly one mole of silver.

Faraday calculations use the ionic charge to connect electrons to products. Forming one mole of a metal of charge n+ needs n moles of electrons, so the mass of metal deposited is found by working out the moles of electrons from Q = I t, dividing by n, and multiplying by the molar mass. This is how the mass of metal deposited or gas released is calculated from the current and the time.
objectives: Use Q = I t to calculate the quantity of electricity
State the value of the Faraday constant and what it means
Calculate the mass of metal deposited using the Faraday constant

The Faraday constant is the charge on one mole of electrons, 96 500 coulombs.
The number of moles of electrons transferred equals the charge divided by 96 500.

lessons.title: Industrial Electrolysis
lessons.content:
Electrolysis is used on an industrial scale to make important products. The electrolysis of concentrated brine, a solution of sodium chloride, is called the chlor-alkali process and produces chlorine gas at the anode, hydrogen gas at the cathode, and sodium hydroxide left in the solution, three substances the chemical industry depends on.

Aluminium is extracted by the electrolysis of molten aluminium oxide, because aluminium is too reactive to extract by heating with carbon. The oxide is dissolved in molten cryolite to lower its melting point and save energy, and the cell uses carbon anodes that burn away as the oxide ions are oxidised to oxygen. Copper is purified by electrolysis, with the impure copper as the anode dissolving into solution and pure copper deposited on a thin cathode.

Each industrial cell shows the same principles as a school experiment, scaled up. In the chlor-alkali cell the ions in brine are discharged at the electrodes, in the aluminium cell the oxide is decomposed into aluminium and oxygen, and in copper refining the impure anode loses copper while the pure cathode gains it, leaving the impurities to fall as anode slime.
objectives: Describe the chlor-alkali process and its three products
Explain why aluminium is extracted by electrolysis and the part played by cryolite
Describe how copper is purified by electrolysis

Aluminium is extracted by electrolysing molten aluminium oxide dissolved in molten cryolite, which lowers its melting point.
In copper purification the impure copper is the anode and pure copper is deposited on the cathode.

lessons.title: Reaction Rate Definition and Factors
lessons.content:
The rate of a reaction is the speed at which the reactants are used up or the products are formed, and it is measured as the change in amount per unit time. A fast reaction, such as the fizzing of magnesium in acid, finishes in seconds, while a slow reaction, such as the rusting of iron, takes weeks or months.

Four factors change the rate of a reaction. Raising the temperature makes the particles move faster and collide more often and more energetically, so the rate rises. Increasing the concentration of a solution, or the pressure of a gas, puts more particles in the same space and so increases the frequency of collisions, and increasing the surface area of a solid exposes more particles to the reaction. A catalyst speeds a reaction up by providing an alternative pathway of lower activation energy, and it is not used up.

All four factors work through collision theory, which says that a reaction happens only when particles collide with enough energy and with the correct orientation. Anything that increases the frequency of successful collisions increases the rate, and this is why temperature, concentration, surface area and catalysts all change how quickly a reaction proceeds.
objectives: Define the rate of a reaction
State the four factors that change the rate and how each does so
Explain how each factor increases the frequency of successful collisions
concepts: Rate of reaction: the speed at which reactants are used up or products are formed, measured as the change in amount per unit time.
Raising the temperature, increasing concentration or pressure, increasing surface area, and adding a catalyst all increase the rate.
Collision theory: a reaction happens only when particles collide with enough energy and the correct orientation.

lessons.title: Interpreting Rate Data and Graphs
lessons.content:
The progress of a reaction is followed by measuring the amount of product formed, or reactant left, at intervals, and plotting the results against time. The amount of product formed rises steeply at first, because the reactants are at their highest concentration, and then the rise flattens as the reaction slows, until the curve levels off when the reaction is complete.

The rate of the reaction at any moment is the gradient of the amount-time graph at that point. A steeper gradient means a faster reaction, so the reaction is fastest at the start, when the gradient is steepest, and it has stopped when the graph becomes horizontal. Comparing two curves on the same axes shows the effect of a factor, such as a higher temperature giving a steeper initial gradient and reaching the same final amount sooner.

Graphs can also show the final amount of product. A reaction that uses more of a reactant produces more product, so its curve levels off at a higher value, and the graph of the amount of reactant left falls from the starting amount to zero as the reaction goes to completion.
objectives: Describe the shape of an amount-against-time graph
Relate the gradient of the graph to the rate of reaction
Interpret two curves on the same axes to compare the effects of a factor

The rate of reaction at any moment is the gradient of the amount-time graph, and a steeper gradient means a faster reaction.
A higher temperature gives a steeper initial gradient and reaches the same final amount sooner.

lessons.title: Exothermic and Endothermic Reactions
lessons.content:
A chemical reaction is exothermic if it releases heat energy to its surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings rises, and endothermic if it absorbs heat energy from its surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings falls. Combustion, the neutralisation of an acid and the reaction of a metal with an acid are all exothermic, and dissolving some salts also gives out heat.

Endothermic reactions take in heat. Thermal decomposition, such as heating a metal carbonate to break it down, and photosynthesis are endothermic, and dissolving some salts in water cools the solution. Whether a reaction is exothermic or endothermic depends on the balance between the energy needed to break bonds in the reactants and the energy released when new bonds form in the products.

Energy is always conserved in a chemical reaction. In an exothermic reaction more energy is released when the products' bonds form than was needed to break the reactants' bonds, so the extra is given out, while in an endothermic reaction more energy is absorbed to break bonds than is released, so the reaction takes heat from its surroundings.

Give examples of each kind of reaction
Explain exothermic and endothermic changes in terms of bond breaking and bond making
concepts: Exothermic reaction: releases heat energy to its surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings rises.
Endothermic reaction: absorbs heat energy from its surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings falls.
In an exothermic reaction more energy is released when bonds form than was needed to break the reactants' bonds.

lessons.title: Energy Profile Diagrams
lessons.content:
An energy profile diagram shows how the energy of a reaction changes as the reactants change into products. Energy is plotted on the vertical axis and the progress of the reaction on the horizontal axis. In an exothermic reaction the products are at a lower energy than the reactants, so the line ends lower than it starts, while in an endothermic reaction the products are at a higher energy and the line ends higher.

The hump in the middle of the profile is the activation energy, the minimum energy that colliding particles must have for a reaction to happen. Even an exothermic reaction needs this initial energy before it can begin, which is why a fuel does not catch fire until it is lit. A catalyst lowers the activation energy, so the hump is smaller and a greater proportion of the particles have enough energy to react, which makes the reaction faster.

The overall energy change of the reaction is the difference between the energy of the products and the energy of the reactants. For an exothermic reaction this difference is given out as heat, and for an endothermic reaction it is taken in, and the difference is written as the enthalpy change of the reaction.
objectives: Sketch an energy profile diagram for an exothermic and an endothermic reaction
Define activation energy and show it on the diagram
Explain how a catalyst changes the profile diagram
concepts: Energy profile diagram: a graph of energy against the progress of the reaction, with the products lower than the reactants for an exothermic reaction.
Activation energy: the minimum energy that colliding particles must have for a reaction to happen, shown as the hump in the profile.
A catalyst lowers the activation energy, so the hump is smaller and the reaction is faster.

lessons.title: Calculating Energy Changes
lessons.content:
The energy change of a reaction can be calculated from bond energies or measured by experiment. Bond energy is the energy needed to break one mole of a bond, and in a reaction the total energy change is the energy taken in to break the bonds in the reactants minus the energy given out when the new bonds form in the products.

The calculation uses the equation: energy change equals the total energy of bond breaking minus the total energy of bond making. If bond making gives out more than bond breaking takes in, the value is negative and the reaction is exothermic; if bond breaking takes in more, the value is positive and the reaction is endothermic.

The energy change can also be measured by calorimetry, in which a reaction is carried out in a container and the temperature rise or fall of a known mass of water is recorded. The heat transferred is calculated with the equation heat equals mass times specific heat capacity times temperature change, and this value, adjusted for the number of moles, gives the enthalpy change of the reaction.
objectives: Define bond energy
Calculate an energy change from bond energies
Describe how calorimetry measures an energy change
concepts: Bond energy: the energy needed to break one mole of a bond.
Energy change equals the total energy of bond breaking minus the total energy of bond making.
Calorimetry records the temperature rise or fall of a known mass of water, and heat equals mass times specific heat capacity times temperature change.

lessons.title: Introduction to Hydrocarbons (Alkanes)
lessons.content:
Organic chemistry is the study of carbon-containing compounds. Hydrocarbons are the simplest organic compounds, consisting only of carbon and hydrogen atoms. Alkanes are a family of 'saturated' hydrocarbons, meaning they contain only single covalent bonds between carbon atoms.

The general formula for alkanes is CₙH₂ₙ₊₂. The first four members of the series are Methane (CH₄), Ethane (C₂H₆), Propane (C₃H₈), and Butane (C₄H₁₀). As the carbon chain gets longer, the boiling point and viscosity of the alkane increase. Alkanes are primarily used as fuels because they burn in oxygen to release large amounts of energy, producing carbon dioxide and water.

In the CSEC syllabus, you must be able to name, draw the structural formulas, and describe the properties of these first four alkanes. You should also understand that alkanes are generally unreactive except for combustion and substitution reactions (where a hydrogen atom is replaced by a halogen like chlorine in the presence of UV light).

Carbon atoms form four covalent bonds, which lets them link into long chains. A compound can be written as a molecular formula, an empirical formula, or a structural (displayed) formula that shows every bond. Alkanes form a homologous series: a family with the same general formula whose members differ by a CH₂ unit, share similar chemical reactions, and show a gradual change in boiling point. Their names follow the same IUPAC pattern, with the first four named methane, ethane, propane and butane.

Most hydrocarbons are obtained from petroleum, which is crude oil. Crude oil is separated into useful fractions by fractional distillation: it is vaporised and passed up a fractionating column that is cooler at the top, so light fractions such as refinery gas and petrol condense near the top, while heavy fractions such as bitumen condense near the bottom. Each fraction is still a mixture of compounds with a similar range of boiling points.

Alkenes are a family of 'unsaturated' hydrocarbons that contain a carbon-carbon double bond. Their general formula is CₙH₂ₙ, and the first member is ethene (C₂H₄). Because of the double bond, alkenes are more reactive than alkanes and take part in addition reactions, in which the double bond opens and a small molecule adds across it. For example, ethene reacts with hydrogen to form ethane and with steam to form ethanol.

The bromine-water test distinguishes the two families: bromine water is orange-brown, and an alkene turns it colourless as bromine adds across the double bond, while an alkane leaves it orange-brown.

Name and draw the first four alkanes

lessons.title: Structural Isomerism
lessons.content:
Structural isomerism is a form of isomerism in which compounds have the same molecular formula but different structural arrangements, meaning their atoms are bonded in a different order. Compounds that share a formula but differ in structure are called structural isomers.

Butane has the molecular formula C₄H₁₀ and two structural isomers. One isomer is a straight chain of four carbon atoms; the other is a branched chain of three carbons with a methyl group attached, named 2-Methylpropane. The two isomers differ in shape, so the straight-chain isomer boils at a higher temperature and the branched isomer boils at a lower temperature.

In the CSEC syllabus you must be able to recognise and draw the structural isomers of the first few alkanes. Isomerism explains why a single molecular formula can name more than one compound.

Draw and name the structural isomers of butane

lessons.title: Distinguishing Alkanes and Alkenes
lessons.content:
Alkanes and alkenes are both hydrocarbons, but they can be told apart because an alkane has only single bonds while an alkene contains a carbon-carbon double bond. Alkanes are saturated and alkenes are unsaturated.

The bromine-water test is the standard test for unsaturation. Bromine water is orange-brown. When shaken with an alkane, it leaves bromine water orange-brown because the alkane cannot react with it. When shaken with an alkene, the alkene turns bromine water colourless as bromine adds across the double bond.

So in the CSEC exam, a colour change from orange-brown to colourless means the sample is an alkene, and no colour change means the sample is an alkane.

Describe the bromine-water test for unsaturation

lessons.title: Functional Groups and Their Properties
lessons.content:
A functional group is an atom or group of atoms that gives an organic compound its characteristic chemical reactions. Molecules with the same functional group belong to the same family and react in similar ways.

Three functional groups matter at CSEC level. Ethanol contains the -OH hydroxyl group, which makes it an alcohol. Ethanoic acid contains the -COOH carboxyl group, which makes it a carboxylic acid. Ethyl ethanoate contains the -COO- ester link, which makes it an ester. Ethene contains a carbon-carbon double bond, which makes it an alkene.

Learning to spot a functional group lets you predict how a molecule will behave: the functional group is the part of the molecule that takes part in reactions, while the hydrocarbon part stays mostly unchanged.

Identify the -OH, -COOH and -COO- functional groups

lessons.title: Ethanol and Fermentation
lessons.content:
Ethanol is an alcohol with the formula C₂H₅OH. It is made in two ways. Fermentation uses yeast to turn sugars into ethanol, working without air. Hydration of ethene reacts ethene with steam over a catalyst, an industrial route that is continuous and fast.

Ethanol is a fuel and a solvent. When it burns, combustion gives carbon dioxide and water, which is why ethanol is blended into motor fuels. Oxidation turns ethanol into ethanoic acid, the acid found in vinegar.

In the CSEC syllabus you must be able to describe fermentation and the hydration of ethene, and to name the products when ethanol burns.

State the reactions of ethanol

lessons.title: Ethanoic Acid
lessons.content:
Ethanoic acid is a carboxylic acid with the formula CH₃COOH. It is the acid in vinegar and gives vinegar its sour taste. Ethanoic acid is a weak acid, so it only partly ionises in water.

Like other acids, ethanoic acid reacts with bases to form salts called ethanoates. With sodium hydroxide, it forms sodium ethanoate and water. With a carbonate, it gives a salt, water and carbon dioxide.

In the CSEC syllabus you must be able to describe ethanoic acid as a weak acid, and to write the word equations for its reactions with bases and carbonates.

State the reactions of ethanoic acid

Ethanoic acid reacts with bases to form salts.

lessons.title: Esters, Hydrolysis, and Detergents
lessons.content:
An ester forms when an alcohol reacts with a carboxylic acid, in a reaction called esterification, which is making an ester from an alcohol and an acid. Esterification is catalysed by an acid and produces an ester and water. Esters often have sweet, fruity smells, so they are used to make perfumes and flavourings.

Hydrolysis is the reverse reaction, breaking an ester back into its alcohol and acid, and it is called hydrolysis. Water breaks an ester into an alcohol and an acid. Soaps and detergents are salts of long-chain acids, made by treating fats or oils with an alkali, and they remove grease because one end of the molecule dissolves in water while the other dissolves in oil.

In the CSEC syllabus you must be able to write the word equation for esterification, and to describe hydrolysis and the cleaning action of soaps and detergents.
objectives: Describe esterification and hydrolysis
Relate esters to perfumes and detergents
concepts: An ester forms when an alcohol reacts with a carboxylic acid.
Hydrolysis breaks an ester back into an alcohol and an acid.

lessons.title: Polymers: Definition and Formation
lessons.content:
A polymer is a long chain built from many small molecules. The small molecules that join up are called monomers, and a monomer is a small molecule that joins up. Polythene, for example, is a polymer made from the monomer ethene.

There are two kinds of polymerisation. Addition polymerisation joins monomers without losing any atoms, so the polymer is the only product. Condensation polymerisation joins monomers while water is also produced, because a small molecule such as water is given off as well.

In the CSEC syllabus you must be able to define a polymer and a monomer, and to describe addition polymerisation and condensation polymerisation.

Distinguish addition and condensation polymerisation

lessons.title: Polymer Uses
lessons.content:
Different polymers have different properties, and the properties decide the uses. Polythene is flexible, light and a good insulator, so it is used to make plastic bags and cling film. PVC (polyvinyl chloride) is tougher, so it is used to make pipes and cable insulation.

Nylon is strong and hard-wearing, so it is used to make ropes and fishing line. The reason one polymer suits a job better than another comes down to how its chains pack together and how strongly they attract.

In the CSEC syllabus you must be able to relate a polymer's properties to its uses, and to name the uses of polythene, PVC and nylon.

A polymer's properties decide what it is used for.

lessons.title: Physical and Chemical Properties of Metals
lessons.content:
Metals share a set of physical properties that make them easy to recognise. Metals have a shiny lustre when freshly cut or polished. Metals are good conductors of heat and electricity. Metals are malleable, so they can be hammered into sheets, and metals are ductile, so they can be drawn into wires. A physical property is one that can be observed without changing the metal into a new substance.

The chemical properties of metals show up in the way they react. Metals react with oxygen to form basic oxides, and a metal oxide that dissolves in water gives an alkaline solution. Metals react with dilute acids to release hydrogen gas, and the more reactive the metal, the faster and more vigorous the reaction is. A chemical property is seen only when the metal takes part in a reaction, and metals always lose electrons to form positive ions.

The most reactive metals tarnish quickly in air and react with cold water, while the least reactive metals, such as gold, stay shiny for centuries because they do not react with oxygen at all. This spread of reactivity is the basis of the reactivity series, and it also explains why different metals are extracted from their ores in different ways.

Describe the chemical properties of metals

lessons.title: Reactions of Metallic Compounds
lessons.content:
Metallic compounds are the oxides, hydroxides and carbonates formed when a metal combines with a non-metal or a polyatomic ion. A metal oxide and metal hydroxide are basic, and they react with acids to form a salt and water: copper(II) oxide is a basic oxide, and sodium hydroxide is an alkali when it dissolves in water.

A metal carbonate reacts with dilute acids to form a salt, water and carbon dioxide gas. The gas can be identified by bubbling it through limewater, which turns milky. Carbonates of the less reactive metals also break down when they are heated: copper(II) carbonate decomposes on heating to form copper(II) oxide and carbon dioxide, and this is called thermal decomposition.

The action of heat on a metallic compound is a useful way to tell how reactive its metal is. The carbonates and hydroxides of the very reactive metals, such as sodium and potassium, do not decompose on heating in the laboratory, while those of the less reactive metals, such as copper, decompose easily. This trend is another face of the reactivity series.

Describe the reaction of metal carbonates with acids and their thermal decomposition
Relate the decomposition of a metallic compound to the reactivity of its metal

Metal carbonates react with dilute acids to form a salt, water and carbon dioxide gas.
The carbonates of the less reactive metals decompose on heating, which is called thermal decomposition.

lessons.title: Reactivity Series of Metals
lessons.content:
The reactivity series is a list of metals arranged in order of how readily they lose electrons and react. At the top of the series, potassium and sodium react violently with cold water, while calcium and magnesium react more slowly. The metals aluminium, zinc, iron and lead sit in the middle of the series, and they react with dilute acids but not with cold water, though zinc and iron react with steam.

Below hydrogen in the series are copper, silver and gold, and they do not react with dilute acids at all. Hydrogen is placed in the series as a reference point: a metal above hydrogen is more reactive than hydrogen and displaces hydrogen from a dilute acid, while a metal below hydrogen is less reactive than hydrogen and will not. Copper, silver and gold are found free in the earth because they are so unreactive.

The series is used to predict displacement reactions. A more reactive metal will displace a less reactive metal from a solution of its salt: iron displaces copper from copper(II) sulphate solution, and the blue solution fades as the copper is deposited. The reverse does not happen, because a less reactive metal cannot displace a more reactive one from its compound.

Explain why hydrogen is used as a reference point in the series
Predict displacement reactions between a metal and a salt solution

lessons.title: Extraction of Aluminium and Iron
lessons.content:
Aluminium is extracted from its ore bauxite, which is mainly aluminium oxide, by electrolysis. The aluminium oxide is dissolved in molten cryolite to lower its very high melting point, and the mixture is electrolysed in a cell lined with carbon. Aluminium forms at the negative electrode and is tapped off, while oxygen forms at the positive electrode and reacts with the carbon anodes, which have to be replaced. This is called the Hall-Heroult process.

Iron is extracted from its ores haematite and magnetite, which are oxides of iron, in a blast furnace. The furnace is charged with iron ore, coke and limestone, and a blast of hot air is blown in. The coke burns to form carbon monoxide, which reduces the iron oxide to molten iron, while the limestone removes the sandy impurities as slag. The molten iron is tapped from the bottom of the furnace.

The two extractions differ because of the reactivity of the metal. Aluminium is too reactive to be reduced by carbon, so it needs electrolysis, which is expensive. Iron is less reactive and can be reduced by carbon monoxide, so the blast furnace is cheaper. Both processes show that the method of extraction depends on the metal's position in the reactivity series.

Describe the extraction of iron in the blast furnace
Explain why aluminium and iron are extracted by different methods

The method of extraction depends on the metal's position in the reactivity series.

lessons.title: Metal Alloys and Uses
lessons.content:
An alloy is a mixture of a metal with one or more other elements, usually other metals or carbon. Alloys are made because they are often stronger and more useful than the pure metals they come from. The atoms of the added element have a different size, so they break up the regular layers of metal atoms and stop the layers from sliding over each other, which is why an alloy is harder than the pure metal.

Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc, used for door fittings and musical instruments. Bronze is an alloy of copper and tin, used for statues and coins. Steel is an alloy of iron with a little carbon, used for construction. Stainless steel contains chromium and nickel, which resist rusting, so it is used for cutlery and sinks. Duralumin is an aluminium alloy used in aircraft because it is light and strong.

The choice of alloy depends on the job it has to do. Steel is used for the framework of buildings because it is strong and cheap, brass is used for taps because it resists corrosion and polishes well, and stainless steel is used in hospitals and kitchens because it resists rusting and is easy to clean.

Name common alloys and the metals they contain
Relate the use of an alloy to its properties

lessons.title: Corrosion of Metals
lessons.content:
Corrosion is the slow destruction of a metal by reaction with its surroundings, and rusting is the corrosion of iron. Iron rusts only when both oxygen and water are present, because the rusting of iron is an oxidation reaction that needs air and moisture. Salt water speeds up rusting, which is why cars rust faster near the sea, and acidic conditions speed it up too.

Rust is a flaky, reddish-brown solid that falls away and exposes fresh iron to attack, so once rusting starts it keeps going until the iron is eaten away. Rusting is expensive because it weakens bridges, ships and pipes, and it can be prevented by keeping air and water away from the iron.

The main methods of preventing rust are painting, oiling or greasing, which coat the iron to keep out air and water, and galvanising, which coats the iron with zinc. Painting coats the iron with a layer of paint to keep out air and water, while oiling or greasing coats moving parts to keep out air and water. Zinc protects the iron even when the coating is scratched, because zinc is more reactive than iron and corrodes instead, which is called sacrificial protection.

Explain why rusting is a problem
Describe the main methods of preventing rust

lessons.title: Impact of Metals on Living Systems
lessons.content:
Some metals are essential to living things, because the body needs them in small amounts to work properly. Iron is needed to make haemoglobin, which carries oxygen in the blood, calcium builds bones and teeth, and zinc is needed for growth and for healing wounds. These are called essential metals, and a shortage of any of them causes illness.

Other metals are toxic, because they poison the body even in tiny amounts. Lead damages the brain and the nervous system, and mercury poisons the kidneys and the brain. Lead and mercury build up in the body instead of being removed, which is why they are so dangerous.

The harm a metal does depends on the dose and on how it gets into the body. Toxic metals can enter through contaminated food or water, or through the skin, and once inside they build up in the tissues. Essential metals are safe only in the right amounts, so too much iron or zinc is harmful too: the dose matters for every metal.

lessons.title: Physical and Chemical Properties of Non-Metals
lessons.content:
Non-metals share a set of physical properties that contrast with those of metals. Non-metals are usually dull and do not have a shiny lustre, and non-metals are poor conductors of heat and electricity. Most non-metals are brittle when solid and have low melting and boiling points, and they exist as gases, liquids or dull solids at room temperature. A physical property is one that can be observed without changing the substance into something new.

The chemical properties of non-metals show up in the way they react. Non-metals react with metals to form ionic compounds, and they gain electrons to form negative ions. Non-metals react with oxygen to form acidic oxides, and an acidic oxide dissolves in water to give an acidic solution. A chemical property is seen only when the non-metal takes part in a reaction.

Non-metals vary a great deal in reactivity. The halogens, such as fluorine and chlorine, are very reactive, while the noble gases, such as helium and neon, hardly react at all. This spread of reactivity explains why non-metals are found both free and combined in nature.

lessons.title: Laboratory Preparation and Uses of Gases
lessons.content:
Gases are prepared in the laboratory from reactions chosen to release them cleanly. Oxygen is prepared by decomposing hydrogen peroxide with manganese(IV) oxide, which acts as a catalyst and speeds the reaction up. Hydrogen is prepared by adding zinc to dilute hydrochloric acid, and carbon dioxide is prepared by adding dilute hydrochloric acid to calcium carbonate.

Chlorine is prepared by oxidising concentrated hydrochloric acid with manganese(IV) oxide. Each gas is collected by a method that suits it: oxygen and hydrogen, which are only slightly soluble in water, are collected over water, while chlorine is collected by upward delivery because it is denser than air.

These gases have important uses. Oxygen is used in hospitals and in oxy-acetylene welding, hydrogen is used to make margarine and ammonia, and carbon dioxide is used in fizzy drinks and in fire extinguishers. Chlorine is used to kill bacteria in water treatment and to make bleach.

lessons.title: Uses of Non-Metals and Compounds
lessons.content:
Non-metals and their compounds are used all around us. Nitrogen fills food packaging to keep food fresh, because it is unreactive and pushes out the oxygen that would let the food spoil. Chlorine kills bacteria in drinking water and in swimming pools, which makes the water safe to drink and to swim in.

Carbon is used in many forms. Graphite, a form of carbon, is used in pencils and as electrodes, while diamond is used in cutting tools because it is the hardest natural substance. Sulphur is used to make sulphuric acid and to vulcanise rubber, which makes the rubber tougher and more elastic.

Compounds of non-metals are just as useful as the elements themselves. Ammonia is used to make fertilisers, which help crops grow, and sulphuric acid is used in car batteries and in the manufacture of many other chemicals.

lessons.title: Environmental Impact of Non-Metals
lessons.content:
When fuels burn, the non-metal oxides they release damage the environment. Carbon dioxide is a greenhouse gas that traps heat in the atmosphere, which contributes to global warming. Carbon monoxide is a poisonous gas that reduces the amount of oxygen the blood can carry, and it forms when fuels burn without enough air.

Sulphur dioxide and the oxides of nitrogen are acidic gases. Sulphur dioxide dissolves in rain water to form acid rain, and the oxides of nitrogen from car exhausts also form acid rain and smog. Acid rain damages buildings, kills fish in lakes and harms trees and crops.

These problems are reduced by burning fuels more cleanly. Removing sulphur from fuels before they are burned, fitting catalytic converters to cars and burning less fuel all reduce the oxides that reach the air. The same gases show that burning fossil fuels has a real cost to the environment.

Explain how carbon monoxide harms the body

lessons.title: Unique Properties of Water
lessons.content:
Water has a set of properties that make it essential for life. Water has a high specific heat capacity, so it heats up and cools down slowly, which keeps the temperature of the oceans and of our bodies steady. Water is an excellent solvent, so it dissolves many substances, which is why it carries dissolved nutrients around the body.

Water is unusual because ice is less dense than liquid water, so ice floats on water. This happens because water expands when it freezes, and it is why ponds freeze from the top down while fish survive underneath. Water also has a high surface tension, so small insects can walk on water without sinking.

These properties depend on the shape of the water molecule and on the hydrogen bonds between water molecules. The hydrogen bonds hold the molecules together, which explains the high boiling point, the high specific heat capacity and the fact that ice floats.

Explain why ice floats on water

lessons.title: Solvent Properties and Water Hardness
lessons.content:
Water is an excellent solvent, so it dissolves many substances and is called the universal solvent. As water runs through the ground it dissolves minerals. Hard water contains dissolved calcium and magnesium salts. Soft water contains few dissolved minerals, and soft water lathers easily with soap.

Hardness has two kinds. Temporary hardness is caused by dissolved calcium hydrogencarbonate, and it is removed by boiling, because boiling decomposes the hydrogencarbonate and the calcium carbonate settles out. Permanent hardness is caused by dissolved calcium sulphate, and it is not removed by boiling.

Hard water is a nuisance because it does not lather easily with soap, so more soap is wasted, and because it leaves scale in kettles and pipes when it is heated. Hard water is softened by boiling, for temporary hardness, or by adding washing soda or by ion exchange, which removes the calcium and magnesium ions.

lessons.title: Water Treatment for Domestic Use
lessons.content:
Water from rivers and reservoirs is treated before it reaches the home. The first stage is screening, which removes large debris such as leaves and sticks, and then the water passes into a settling tank, where sedimentation lets the heavier particles settle to the bottom.

After sedimentation the water is filtered. Filtration removes solid particles by passing the water through beds of sand and gravel. The final stage is chlorination, where a little chlorine is added, which kills bacteria and germs and makes the water safe to drink.

Fluoride is sometimes added to help protect teeth, and the treated water is stored in covered reservoirs and pumped through pipes to homes. Each stage removes something different, and together they make the water clear and safe to drink.

lessons.title: Green Chemistry Principles
lessons.content:
Green chemistry is a way of designing chemical processes that produce less waste and use safer substances. The first principle is prevention: it is better to prevent waste than to clean it up afterwards. Atom economy means designing reactions so that as many of the reactant atoms as possible end up in the product, leaving little behind.

A less hazardous chemical synthesis designs processes that use and make safer chemicals, so that accidents and exposure are less harmful. Renewable feedstocks use raw materials that can be replaced, such as plant material, instead of those that will run out, such as crude oil.

Energy efficiency runs reactions at room temperature and pressure wherever possible, so less energy is used, and catalysis uses catalysts to speed reactions up without the need for extra chemicals. Together these principles cut waste, save energy and reduce the hazards of the chemical industry.

lessons.title: Identification of Cations
lessons.content:
Cations are positive ions, and they are identified by the colour they give to a flame or by the precipitates they form with sodium hydroxide. In a flame test, a clean wire is dipped in the salt and held in a blue flame. Sodium gives a yellow flame, potassium gives a lilac flame, and calcium gives a brick-red flame.

Copper(II) gives a blue-green flame. When sodium hydroxide solution is added to a solution of a salt, the precipitate identifies the cation: copper(II) gives a blue precipitate with sodium hydroxide, iron(II) gives a green precipitate, and iron(III) gives a brown precipitate.

Ammonium is identified by warming the salt with sodium hydroxide, which releases ammonia gas that turns damp red litmus paper blue. The flame test and the sodium hydroxide test are the two standard ways of identifying a cation in the laboratory.

lessons.title: Identification of Anions
lessons.content:
Anions are negative ions, and each has a test that identifies it. A carbonate fizzes with dilute acid, and the gas released turns limewater milky. This is the test for a carbonate.

A chloride gives a white precipitate with silver nitrate solution, and the precipitate dissolves in dilute ammonia. A sulphate gives a white precipitate with barium chloride solution, and this precipitate does not dissolve in acid. The two white precipitates are told apart by what dissolves them.

A nitrate is identified by the brown ring test: iron(II) sulphate solution is added, then concentrated sulphuric acid is poured carefully down the side, and a brown ring forms where the two liquids meet.

Describe the tests for chloride and sulphate, and how they are told apart
Describe the brown ring test for a nitrate

lessons.title: Identification of Gases
lessons.content:
Gases are identified by simple tests that give a clear result. Oxygen relights a glowing splint, and hydrogen burns with a squeaky pop when a lighted splint is held to it. These two tests tell oxygen and hydrogen apart from the other gases.

Carbon dioxide turns limewater milky when it is bubbled through it. Chlorine bleaches damp blue litmus paper, and it has a sharp, choking smell. These tests use a glowing splint, limewater and litmus paper, which are the standard ways of identifying a gas.

Ammonia turns damp red litmus paper blue, and it has a sharp smell. Each gas has a test that no other common gas gives, so the tests are used one after another until the gas is identified.

Describe the test for carbon dioxide, chlorine and ammonia
